devised fluorous microgel star polymers designed specifically to capture PFOS and PFOA through hydrophobic interactions. The star polymer’s backbone consists of poly (ethylene glycol) (PEG), providing a hydro-

philic surface that attracts PFOA and PFOS molecules. Meanwhile, the core of the star polymer is fluorinated, enhancing hydrophobic in-teractions to immobilize PFOA and PFOS within the polymer structure. These captured contaminants can be released by treatment with organic solvents or salts. However, fluorous microgel star polymers face chal-lenges: they cannot be easily reused due to the micelle structure being susceptible to environmental disruption. Moreover, the star polymers exist in an unstable liquid phase, which complicates their application on a large scale \[[131](#_bookmark144)\].

Therefore, there is an urgent need to develop new sorbents for PFAS removal that offer easy regeneration, short equilibrium times, high sorption capacities, and reusability. The PEGDA amination presents electrostatic forces, while the PEGDA fluoridation improves hydropho-bic interactions. PEGDA bifunctionalization combines both fluoridation and amination, thereby simultaneously leveraging hydrophobic in-teractions and electrostatic forces. This research aims to assess the ef-

ficacy of these functionalization’s in removing long-chain (PFOS and

PFOA), short-chain fluorinated substances (PFBS and PFBA), and per-fluoroalkyl ether carboxylic acids (such as GenX) from wastewater. Additionally, the study investigates methods for regenerating the func-tionalized PEGDA materials after use \[[26](#_bookmark41)\].

- 1.  _Hydrophilic interactions_

PFASs are synthetic compounds known for their unique hydrophobic

molecules, the hydrophobic interaction significantly aids in PFAS sorption onto specific sorbent materials \[[128](#_bookmark141)\]. Hydrophobic in-teractions within hydrogels contribute significantly to their mechanical strength, thereby enhancing their suitability for diverse applications \[[129](#_bookmark142)\]. The process involves copolymerizing hydrophobic segments within a hydrophilic polymer matrix. Initially, these hydrophobic re-gions serve as physical cross-linking sites during the reaction initiation. As the reaction progresses, these sites interact with other hydrophilic

and hydrophilic properties and low surface tension. Recently, there has been growing interest in novel materials utilizing natural and synthetic polymer sorbents for remediating PFAS in aqueous systems. Hydrogels are highly efficient water retention compounds. Hydrophilic polymers grow when submerged in water that maintain chemical and structural integrity.

PFOA/PFOS molecules are bound to the hydrophilic PEG surface, which forms the backbone structure of the starpolymer. In contrast, the star polymer core is composed of fluorinated segments that enhance

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Fig. 8.** Mechanisms of elimination of pollutants by hydrogels.

hydrophobic interactions and include PFOA and PFOS. It is possible to release the encapsulated PFOA/PFOS by adding organic solvents or salts to the polymer material \[[131](#_bookmark144)\]. Hydrogel-based sorbents have a tendency to easily spread water-polluting chemicals over the hydrogel matrix via its hydrophilic properties. One of the constituents used to make hydrogel-based sorbent materials is PEGDA. This can be addressed by the hydrophilic PEG backbone and its presence of diacrylate groups, which enable customized functionality \[[26](#_bookmark41)\].

Umarasamy and colleagues presented a novel approach to the fabrication of PFAA-targeting adsorbents. They crafted hydrogels while encasing the PFAA molecule in their aqueous solution to attract and retain the dissolved chemical substance molecules. The subsequent functional groups were contemporary in these hydrogels: charged, hy-

drophobic, hydrophilic, and fluorinated. The hydrogel’s capacity to

absorb water was improved by illustration the negatively charged PFAA molecular group into the positively charged hydrophilic chemical groups. Likewise, the fluorinated segments were engineered to reject non-fluorinated organic molecules and draw in additional fluorinated ones. The charged groups may be systematically changed to optimize the

hydrogel’s capacity to absorb PFAA since the network is modular. This

strategy is an example of a flexible way to make tailored adsorbents that might be used to remove PFAA contaminants from aquatic environments \[[56](#_bookmark71)\].

- 1.  _Ion-exchange-based interaction_

Ion exchange is critical to the adsorption process when hydrogels and contaminants have basic or acidic functional groups. Ion exchange comprehends the role of chemisorption, or the process of forming a chemical link between pollutant ions and the functional groups on the hydrogel surface. This interaction aids in the more efficient removal of pollutants by facilitating ion exchange between pollutant molecules and the hydrogel surface functional groups. Compared to other adsorbents as AC, the anion-exchange resin Amberlite-IRA67 shows a better removal efficacy of short-chain PFAS. The effectiveness of this process is due to the abundance of amine groups on the resin surface, which facilitate anion exchange mechanisms during adsorption. Anion exchange pre-dominantly governs the PFCAs adsorption on IRA67 ion exchange resin. The elimination percentages of three PFCAs increase with higher resin

doses. Interestingly, the removal efficiencies still follow the order PFHxA < PFHpA < PFOA, despite this increase. This suggests that

intraparticle diffusion does not restrict the process. Instead, the forma-tion of hemi-micelles and micelles likely plays a pivotal role in the enhanced removal of long-chain PFCAs \[[110](#_bookmark123)\].

- 1.  _Electrostatic interactions_

Efficient electrostatic interactions occur in systems where the hydrogel surface charge is opposite to that of the pollutant. These in-teractions facilitate the formation of polymer-nanoparticle hybrid hydrogels, enhancing both the mechanical properties of the hydrogels and the interaction strength within the polymer structure. Electrostatic attraction is the primary mechanism for sorbing PFASs onto function-alized PEGDA sorbents. Enhancing the sorption capacity for PFAS, particularly soluble anionic PFASs, can therefore be achieved by increasing the _ζ_\-potential of functionalized PEGDA sorbents. Unmodi-fied PEGDA typically has a negative _ζ_\-potential, whereas MTAC-modified PEGDA shifts this to positive. Adjusting the concentration of MTAC during synthesis enables the production of functionalized PEGDA

with higher ζ-potential. Additionally, it has been observed that at low

pH levels, the sorption capabilities for PFOS and PFOA are enhanced. Conversely, the presence of ions such as Ca2+ and Na+ has been found to interfere with the absorption of PFASs \[[132](#_bookmark145)\].

When the solution pH is greater than the point of zero charge (pHpzc), the ferro-gel exhibits a negative (—Ve) surface charge, leading to electrostatic repulsion with negatively charged pollutants.

Conversely, when the pH of the solution is lower than the pHpzc, fer-rogel acquires a positive surface charge. This results in electrostatic attraction between the anionic form of the pollutant and the positively charged ferrogel surface. Molecular dynamics simulations investigate how GenX, a representative short-chain PFAS compound, adsorbs onto a polycationic hydrogel with varying degrees of fluorination in its back-bone and cross-linkers. The simulations reveal that the optimal adsorption environment for GenX is achieved when fluorinated seg-ments are adjacent to cationic groups within the polymer gel structure. This arrangement enhances the binding of GenX molecules through a synergistic combination of electrostatic and hydrophobic interactions facilitated by the cationic-fluorophilic segments. In contrast, polymer segments lacking fluorination or cationic charges do not exhibit com-parable binding efficiency. Additionally, the gel displays strong selec-tivity for GenX over its hydrogenated counterpart \[[133](#_bookmark146)\].

- 1.  _π_–_π interaction_

This particular interaction is exclusive to contaminants and/or ad-sorbents that incorporate aromatic rings into their structures. Numerous pollutants contain nitroaromatic rings and polycyclic aromatic moieties,

which exhibit both π-acceptor and π-donor properties. These PFAS

compounds and adsorbents can also exhibit varying charges depending

on the pH conditions. PFAS compounds can be adsorbed onto adsorbents

through various mechanisms such as hydrophobic and electrostatic ef-fects, hydrogen bonding, and π–π bonding. CTAB, distinguished by its quaternary ammonium group and long alkyl chain, has been selected for its ability to enhance the adsorbent’s affinity towards PFAS. This enhancement is primarily achieved through strengthened hydrophobic

and electrostatic interactions.

- 1.  _Hydrogen bonding_

Hydrogen bonding is a predominant force influencing the adsorption mechanisms of water pollutants by hydrogels. PFOA is removed from solutions through adsorption onto alginate hydrogel. The primary mechanisms facilitating PFOA removal by the hydrogel include hydrogen bonding, electrostatic interactions, and hydrophobic in-teractions \[[101](#_bookmark114)\].

- 1.  _Electrochemical oxidation (EO)_

The study investigates nanoparticle-embedded hydrogel synthesized electrodes for the EO of PFOS and PFOA. EO processes facilitate PFOS and PFOA removal by generating •OH radicals, which potentially induce decarboxylation or defluorination reactions.

The PFOA and PFOS carbon chains are broken down sequentially by these mechanisms, yielding carbon dioxide (_CO_2), fluoride (_F_—), and sulfate (_SO_—2) as the final products. _CO_2 and _HF_ precipitate as a result of Kolbe decarboxylating the perfluorinated alkyl radicals to which PFOA directly transfers electrons. Similar mechanisms such hydrolysis, radical reactions, and Kolbe decarboxylation are involved in the breakdown of PFOS. Using NPs-PAA/PAH embedded electrodes, the work shows that

4

the removal efficacy of PFOS is 1.7–2.7 times greater than that of PFOA,

highlighting the significance of •_OH_ radicals in the electrochemical

breakdown of both compounds \[[23](#_bookmark38)\].

- 1.  _Adsorption kinetics and isotherms_

Kinetic profiles play a vital role in the design and operation of adsorption-based wastewater treatment systems, as they provide valu-able insights into adsorption rates, equilibrium times, mass transfer mechanisms, and the efficiency of adsorbents \[[134](#_bookmark147)\]. Factors such as pH, temperature, particle size, and porosity of adsorbents have a significant impact on the kinetics of PFAS adsorption \[[135](#_bookmark148)\]. Several kinetic models,

including the pseudo-first-order, pseudo-second-order, and Elovich models, have been used to predict the adsorption behavior of PFAS on materials like hydrogels. Many studies have shown that the pseudo-second-order model is the most suitable for describing the kinetics of PFAS adsorption, suggesting that chemisorption is the rate-limiting step ([Table 2](#_bookmark12)). This emphasizes the need to account for the unique in-teractions between adsorbents and adsorbates when choosing the most appropriate kinetic model.

Equilibrium isotherms play a crucial role in determining the maximum adsorption capacity of adsorbents and in understanding the interactions between adsorbate and adsorbent. The widely used Lang-muir and Freundlich isotherm models have been thoroughly evaluated to predict the adsorption equilibrium of PFAS on hydrogels. Several studies have indicated that the Langmuir model effectively describes the equilibrium adsorption of PFAS such as PFOA, PFOS, PFBS, PFHxS, PFHxA, PFHpA, and GenX, based on the assumption that a monolayer of adsorbate is formed and no additional adsorption can take place at occupied sites. However, other research suggests that the Freundlich model provides a better fit for PFAS adsorption on hydrogels, as it ac-counts for heterogeneous adsorption energies on the adsorbent surface and the formation of multilayers through dispersive interactions \[[136](#_bookmark149)\] ([Table 2](#_bookmark12)). All of these factors play a critical role in determining the mechanism of PFAS adsorption on hydrogels and their composites.

# Future directions for enhancing PFAS sorption and removal efficiency

Developing practical water treatment solutions necessitates research intensive on increasing the PFAS sorption and removal efficiency, pre-dominantly in interpretation of the escalating environmental appre-hensions. Using eco-friendly resources like biomass (agriculture, industrial, household etc.), clay (red clay etc.), and coagulant (alum, clay etc.) mediated hydrogels have thoughtful optimistic impact on the environment and economic benefits. These materials are typically cost-

effective and do not produce side product. Furthermore, bioflocculants/ biocoagulants generate biodegradable sludge that is ecologically safe, diminishing the overall environmental. Therefore, their adoption pro-motes a cleaner, healthier environment and sustainability, while also lessening the environmental impact of traditional chemicals. ([Fig. 9](#_bookmark15)).

Additional research is required in order to precisely assess hydrogels’

capacity for PFAS and PFAA decontamination. A thorough technological-economic research program on material preparation (en-ergy cost, commercialization etc.), lifespan (Reusability etc.), waste generation (byproduct etc.), and waste management (local or interna-tional policies etc.) should be carried out. These hydrogels ought to be compared with well-known substitutes such granular activated carbon. Notably, the synthesis of hydrogels must be relatively straightfor-ward, allowing for kilogram-scale production. To maximize its envi-ronmental impact, further refinement of the technique (such as 3D

printing) is necessary. Despite these challenges, the material’s scalabil-

ity and efficiency make hydrogels one of the most effective options for adsorbing various PFAS compounds.

Looking ahead, the development of porous hydrogels, such as those based on trianglamine, marks a significant advancement in PFAS remediation technologies. By incorporating permanent positive charges through quaternization, these hydrogels demonstrate exceptional sorp-tion kinetics for both long- and short-chain PFAS with diverse functional groups, all while maintaining non-toxicity and excellent chemical stability.

Future research should focus on refining hydrogel architectures by optimizing charge distribution and engineering hierarchical porosity to enhance selectivity and adsorption capacity, particularly for challenging ultrashort-chain PFAS. This technology holds immense potential for real-world applications, ranging from point-of-use filtration systems to large-scale industrial wastewater treatment and in-situ groundwater remediation using injectable hydrogel formulations or permeable reac-tive barriers.

A key avenue for progress lies in developing sustainable regeneration

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Fig. 9.** Recycling of different biomass for useful purposes.

strategies that minimize environmental impact, possibly through the use of green solvents or electrochemical techniques to restore adsorption capacity. Additionally, integrating advanced oxidation processes could facilitate complete PFAS mineralization. To ensure practical imple-mentation, rigorous life-cycle assessments and comparative studies against conventional adsorbents are essential, alongside efforts to secure regulatory approvals and industry collaborations for commercialization. Addressing emerging challenges will require systematic investiga-tion of competitive sorption effects in complex water matrices and long-term stability under real-world conditions. As research advances, hydrogel-based systems have the potential to evolve into a scalable, versatile platform for comprehensive PFAS management, seamlessly combining efficient capture with sustainable regeneration or destruction pathways. Their unique blend of high performance and environmental safety positions them as a promising cornerstone solution in global ef-forts to mitigate persistent PFAS contamination across diverse envi-

ronmental settings.

To optimize performance in a variety of techniques, future research should look at how pH and other ions affect the adsorption capacity adsorbents. To increase the metal anions adsorption and removal ability, future research should be focused on enhancing its structure and composition of hydrogels. Such as introduction of the functional groups like Sulfonic or carboxyl groups might be added to hydrogels to perhaps improve its absorption capacity.

To fully comprehend and improve this mechanism, NMR spectros-copy investigation is required to confirm the degree of fluorination. Future studies ought to assess hybrid approaches that make use of several interaction kinds in order to enhance PFAS sorption capacity and

removal effectiveness. More research is necessary, especially to examine the special performance of fluorine–fluorine interactions in sorption selectivity.

Determining that environmental and public health standards are followed during production, consumption, and recycling processes should be a goal of study. Identifying the interplay between hydrogels and organic matter will be vital for developing solutions that reduce the damaging impacts of PFAS on the environment.

# Integration of quantum computational insights into PFAS sorption studies

The integration of experimental and computational methods has greatly enhanced the understanding of _PFAS_ sorption mechanisms. Quantum mechanical simulations, such as density functional theory (DFT) valued for its balance between accuracy and computational effi-ciency and ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD), offer atomic-level in-sights that supplement experimental findings. Ilango and colleagues employed DFT modeling to investigate molecular-level interactions be-tween _GTH_ —_CTNPEI_ aerogel and _PFAS_. Their DFT-based mechanistic analysis identified strong stabilizing hydrophobic and electrostatic in-teractions between the aerogels and PFAS, with binding energies

ranging from: —24.0 to —30.1_kcal_/_mol_ for _PFOA_, —41.3 to

—48.5_kcal_/_mol_ for _PFOS_, and —40.5 to —47.3 kcal/mol for _PFBS_. These findings highlight the material’s strong potential for PFAS removal from drinking water, surface water, and groundwater. The dominant elec-

trostatic interactions occur between protonated amine groups (_NH_+) in the sorbents (_CTN_ and _PEI_) and anionic _PFAS_ headgroups (_COO_—/_SO_—), while hydrophobic interactions primarily involve the fluorinated carbon chains \[[137](#_bookmark150)\].

3

3

Moreover, simulations incorporating solvation models (e.g., _SMD_) have elucidated the influence of water and competing anions (e.g., _Cl_—, _SO_2—) on _PFAS_ removal efficiency, corroborating experimental findings

4

in tap water. However, most DFT studies on _PFAS_ to date have relied on conventional computational approaches, which only examine static, time-independent properties near stationary points on the _PFAS_ poten-tial energy surface. While static DFT calculations are limited to equi-

librium properties, quantum dynamics methods inherently capture time-dependent, nonequilibrium phenomena \[[138](#_bookmark151)\].

Biswas & Wong employed _AIMD_ simulations to demonstrate that PFAS degradation on γ-Al2O3 surfaces is temperature-dependent and

facilitated by oxygen vacancies, providing a mechanistic explanation for experimental thermal treatment results. Their _AIMD_ calculations revealed that these simulations can not only predict secondary byproducts but also prescreen the conditions required for efficient contaminant remediation. Large-scale _AIMD_ simulations further un-covered distinct degradation pathways for _PFOA_ on different adsorbent surfaces. Critically, the study showed that fluorine atoms from PFOA become mineralized on the adsorbent surface, thereby preventing their release into the surrounding environment \[[139](#_bookmark152)\].

By explicitly incorporating temperature effects and atomistic surface details, _AIMD_ simulations provide critical mechanistic insights that extend beyond conventional static DFT calculations. Unlike DFT, which neglects temperature, _AIMD_ reveals the specific conditions required for efficient _PFOA_ degradation. Future research should incorporate quan-tum computational insights into _PFAS_ sorption studies by integrating static and dynamic simulation approaches, developing multiscale models, experimentally validating predictions, and extending simula-tions to various _PFAS_ structures and environmental conditions.

# Perspectives and conclusions

This review article emphasizes on how important hydrogel-based adsorbents are for the treatment of PFAS wastewater. Due to enduring nature and health hazards impacts, PFAS chemicals pose a great trans-action of difficulty and require efficient elimination techniques. With high adsorption capabilities that typically approach such as 500 mg/g and outstrip many other conventional materials, hydrogels have been emerged as an intriguing option. Hydrogel adsorbents are consequently attractive options for widespread use in the treatment of wastewater polluted with PFAS. There are important things to keep in mind notwithstanding these developments. Reusability and regeneration of hydrogel applications are critical to their viability as a means of reducing operating expenses in wastewater treatment plants. Sustain-ability also necessitates careful consideration of efficient techniques for wasted hydrogel disposal and environmental effect minimization. Advanced quantum dynamical methods are essential for investigating PFAS degradation mechanisms. Techniques such as ab initio molecular dynamics, DFT-based metadynamics, high-temperature reactivity studies, and real-time time-dependent DFT enable a deeper under-standing of the inherently dynamic nature of the PFAS degradation process. These methods provide time-resolved insights into dynamical, temperature-dependent, and light-induced effects that conventional DFT calculations cannot capture.

Additionally, whereas the majority of research to far has been on

single-component PFAS adsorption studies, future studies must tackle the complexity of multicomponent PFAS combinations that are frequently encountered in wastewater from real-world sources. Deter-mining the processes behind PFAS adsorption onto hydrogels under various environmental circumstances is still a top concern. Green chemistry and nanoscience research must continue to enhance these technologies. The aforementioned advances are designed to improve the

hydrogel-based wastewater treatment systems’ efficacy, cost, and

environmental acceptability. By overcoming these obstacles, hydrogels have great potential to further the purification of water, especially in controlling the PFAS contamination that poses a persistent hazard.
